newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer says Duisenberg good choice to head ECB.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer says Duisenberg good choice to head ECB.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Sunday choosing Dutch central bank governor Wim Duisenberg as the head of the future European Central Bank (ECB) would be a signal of commitment to stability.
"I believe that Mr Duisenberg really stands for lasting stability," Tietmeyer told German radio.
"In that respect a decision (to appoint him as ECB head) would certainly also be a signal in the right direction," Tietmeyer added. A copy of the radio interview was released in advance.
Tietmeyer also said he had been informed there had been no behind-the-scenes agreement to give France the honour of supplying the first ECB head.

Duisenberg, who officially replaces Alexandre Lamfalussy next week as president of the ECB forerunner, the European Monetary Institute, had a long record as a central banker and had served the Netherlands and the Dutch guilder well, Tietmeyer said.
"He is someone who is convinced that stable money is a crucial basis for a succesful economic development," Tietmeyer said.
"To the extent that he has also proved this, that he can put this into political practice, that he can put this into concrete political practice, that is a good starting point in my opinion."
Tietmeyer said a person who had proved successful in his work so far would be a good candidate for the ECB post.

Asked about talk of a pact for France to put in place a candidate, he said: "I am not aware of such arrangements. On the contrary, I have been told that there is no such arrangement." Markets would pay close attention to the appointment of key figures in the ECB, not only its president, but also the vice-president and the members of its ruling council, Tietmeyer said.
"I am of the opinion that these personnel decisions ought to reflect the line the European Central Bank wants to take.
"I assume that the personnel decisions will also correspond with the goal that is set down in the (Maastricht) Treaty for the European Central Bank, that is -- securing lasting stability."
